questions.knowledge_point: Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069302/assets/9fd222d255fd1a37f00cbe7c9abf6af0d0e3af92f9ac581591bb1062780e69fa.png)

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $ABCA,$ shown in the diagram above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={-{C}_{1}}\cup {C}_{2}\cup {-{C}_{3}},
$$

where $-{C}_{1}$ and $-{C}_{3}$ are the same paths as ${C}_{1}$ and ${C}_{3}$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069302/assets/6087da076e65bda5240c428ff67c570ad59ae9a8e5a5a3c9e8406184998de56a.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(1,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(1,0)$ to the point $B(0,-2).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=\frac{7}{3},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=({x}^{2}+y)\,i+(x-{y}^{2})\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the horizontal line segment from $O$ to $A.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =0+t(a-0) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,0⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,0⟩ \\  & =t\,i,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=t$ and $y=0.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =({x}^{2}+y)\,i+(x-{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =({t}^{2}+0)\,i+(t-{0}^{2})\,j \\  & ={t}^{2}\,i+t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)j \\  & =i\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =({t}^{2}\,i+t\,j)\cdot (i) \\  & ={t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{3} \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0)+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069302/assets/c0a4f042748ddadd824bed4ee71bca9724d7ca7dcc376a0ccf7c1353d59ec4fc.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,2)$ to the point $B(-1,2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(-1,2)$ to the point $D(-1,0).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{7}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x-y)\,i+(y-x)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the vertical line segment from $B$ to $D.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(d-b) \\  & =⟨-1,2⟩+t(⟨-1,0⟩-⟨-1,2⟩) \\  & =⟨-1,2-2t⟩ \\  & =-\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-1$ and $y=2-2t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(x-y)\,i+(y-x)\,j \\  & =(-1-(2-2t))\,i+(2-2t-(-1))\,j \\  & =(-3+2t)\,i+(3-2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-2t)j \\  & =-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =((-3+2t)\,i+(3-2t)\,j)\cdot (-2\,j) \\  & =(3-2t)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4t-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{1}(4t-6)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+[2{t}^{2}-6t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+[2({1}^{2})-6(1)-0] \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}-4 \\  & =-\frac{15}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields
questions.problem: Let $F(x,y,z)=2z\,i+3x\,j-4y\,k$ and let $C$ be a path in ${R}^{3}.$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r?$
questions.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
F(x,y,z)=P(x,y,z)\,i+Q(x,y,z)\,j+R(x,y,z)\,k
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{C}P(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y+R(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore, in our case, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}2z\,\text{d}x+3x\,\text{d}y-4y\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$
